stem: A newborn has an isolated cleft palate. Which feeding plan is most appropriate for the nurse to reinforce with the parents?

options.A: Use a specialized cleft-feeding bottle and obtain feeding support because the infant may not generate adequate suction
options.B: Use an unmodified standard breastfeeding technique because cleft palate does not affect suction
options.C: Avoid all oral feeding until surgical repair is completed
options.D: Use a standard bottle only and enlarge the nipple opening independently until feeding becomes faster

rationale: AAP guidance explains that infants with cleft palate generally suck weakly and often need a special bottle, with support from clinicians experienced in cleft-palate feeding. This differs from many infants with isolated cleft lip, who may breastfeed or use a standard bottle successfully. Complete avoidance of oral feeding is not routine, and parents should not independently modify equipment in a way that could create unsafe flow. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Teach that a newborn with cleft palate often needs specialized feeding equipment and expert feeding support because an intact palate is important for generating effective suction.
source_document_title: Caring for Babies Born with Cleft Lip or Cleft Palate: AAP Report Explained

source_claim_supported: Infants with cleft palate commonly have weak suction and may require a specialized bottle and skilled feeding support.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — Nutrition and Oral Hydration: assess ability to eat/drink and provide feeding assistance or adaptive techniques as needed

correction_summary: Corrected the blueprint from Physiological Adaptation to Basic Care and Comfort, specified isolated cleft palate to prevent confusion with isolated cleft lip, and replaced weak distractors with realistic feeding alternatives while avoiding unsourced device-modification instructions.
audit_findings: A is directly supported by AAP guidance. B is incorrect because cleft palate commonly impairs suction; C is overly restrictive because oral feeding with specialized techniques is commonly used; D encourages unsupervised equipment modification and ignores specialized feeding guidance. No second defensible answer remains. Independent adversarial second pass and NCSBN mapping passed.
